content.text: You don't need NgRx or another store library to share state between Angular components. A service provided in the root injector is already one instance that every component shares; what makes it a store is holding the state in a signal, exposing it read-only and changing it only through methods that create new values. Reach for a library when its conventions and tooling solve a problem you actually have.

The notifications panel has a "Mark as read" button. Click it, and the notification turns grey in the panel, but the bell in the header still says 3. The ticket that comes out of the bug triage reads "Introduce NgRx so components share state correctly", estimated at three days. Yet the header and the panel already inject the same
and read the same signal. The bug is one line:
on an object inside the signal's array, and the signal never finds out.

The belief: Angular components can't really share state on their own. Once two components that aren't parent and child need the same data, you need a store library with actions, reducers and selectors, or the data will drift apart.

It comes from real experience. For years, a store library was the standard answer for shared state in many Angular codebases, and the alternative people saw was often messy: a service with a plain public field that every component mutates directly, and views that sometimes forget to refresh. That chaos is real, and a store library does fix it by putting every change through one path. But the fix doesn't come from the library itself. It comes from three rules the library enforces, and a signal-based service can follow the same three rules in one file.
A root service is already shared

, is provided in the root injector. The services guide lists what that guarantees: a single, shared instance for the whole application, available anywhere without registering a provider. Every component that calls
gets the same object. Sharing was never the hard part.
Angular has to see the change
The hard part is noticing changes. Since Angular 21, apps run without zone.js by default, and since Angular 22 components default to
. The zoneless guide lists what makes Angular run change detection: things like

, a template event listener, or an update to a signal that a template reads. Assigning a plain field on a service is none of those, so the header has no reason to check itself again. Put the value in a
that reads it is notified when it changes.
A signal only knows about new values
That's where the bug in the hook comes from. By default, a signal compares the old and new value with
value, not a changed object. Mutating an item inside the array keeps the same array, so nothing is notified, and a
like the unread count keeps its cached result. The panel happened to re-render, because the click event checked it, which made the bug look like a sharing problem.
The signals guide adds a second warning:

content.text: Not all shared state is app-wide. A wizard, an editor or a dashboard widget often needs state shared by a component and its children, but separate for each instance. Provide the store in that component's
instead: the hierarchical injectors guide notes that each component instance then gets a private instance of the service, which is destroyed with the component. Use
for a store that should only exist where you provide it.

How to apply it in your project

items.title: Find shared state in plain fields

content.text: Look for root services with public mutable fields or arrays. Each one is a view that may not refresh under OnPush and zoneless change detection.

content.text: Search for writes from components, then give each kind of change a method that calls

items.title: Decide when a library earns its place

content.text: If many teams change the same state through complex flows and need conventions or debugging tools to keep it manageable, evaluate a store library for that state. Keep the rest in signal services.
